Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Driving with Others: Driving with people
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Danielle, a twenty-one-year-old electrician, had always been the kind of person who lived in the forward momentum of her work. On a job site, she was known for her steady hands and her ability to read a blueprint and execute it precisely, trusting her instincts and her training without a second thought. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, when she was driving her work van home along a two-lane highway. A sedan ran a red light at an intersection and T-boned the passenger side of her van at nearly fifty miles per hour. The van spun, rolled once, and came to rest on its roof in a drainage ditch. Danielle remembers the sound of tearing metal and the smell of gasoline more clearly than she remembers the impact itself. She was trapped upside down in her harness for twenty-two minutes before the fire department cut her out. She walked away with a fractured wrist and deep bruising, but what stayed with her was the absolute certainty, in those moments hanging upside down, that her body had failed her completely—that she had no control over whether she lived or died.

In the weeks that followed, Danielle returned to work, but something fundamental had shifted. She found herself unable to drive with her usual apprentice, a young man named Marcus who had always been her passenger. The thought of having someone else in the van with her, of being responsible for their safety, made her palms sweat and her chest tighten. She started taking solo service calls only, driving alone and avoiding any route that took her through the intersection where the crash had occurred. On the job, she began to second-guess herself constantly. When wiring a panel, she would check and recheck her connections three or four times, certain that she was about to make a catastrophic mistake. She had come to believe that she could no longer trust her own body to do what she needed it to do, that it might betray her at any moment, just as it had in the crash. The idea that she could be injured or killed through no fault of her own felt deeply unfair, and she found herself replaying the moment the sedan ran the light, wondering why no one had been held accountable, why nothing had been done.

The most insidious trigger, however, was the future. When a supervisor mentioned a promotion track that would require her to manage a small crew in six months, Danielle felt a wave of nausea. Talking about the future—about next year, about where she saw herself in five years—felt like a trap. She was certain that if she allowed herself to plan or hope, something would come along to destroy it. She started avoiding conversations about holidays, about career goals, about anything that required her to imagine a time beyond the next few days. Her friends noticed she had become distant, and her mother worried aloud that Danielle seemed to have lost her spark.

It was a specific moment that finally pushed her to seek help. Marcus, her former apprentice, had been reassigned to another electrician, and he called her one evening to ask if she wanted to grab dinner. As they talked, he mentioned that he was thinking of proposing to his girlfriend, and Danielle felt her throat close. She made an excuse and ended the call, then sat in her apartment, trembling. She realized that she could not even tolerate a friend talking about his own future without feeling like the ground was about to open beneath her. What frightened her most was the growing sense that she was shrinking her life down to a tiny, safe space, and that if she kept going this way, there would be nothing left of the person she used to be. She wanted to trust herself again, to believe that her body could carry her through a workday without disaster, and to let herself imagine a future without waiting for the crash.
